analysis.one_liner: Requires credit card bills to show how long and how costly minimum-only payments are.
analysis.headline: The Credit Card Repayment Act of 2007 never left committee, dying without a vote despite its House introduction, and no one ever recorded a vote for or against it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every credit card statement to tell cardholders, in plain numbers, what making only the minimum payment really costs: how many years and how much total interest it would take to pay off their balance, what payment would clear it in 36 months, and a toll-free number for approved nonprofit credit counseling. It amends the Truth in Lending Act and directs the Federal Reserve and Federal Trade Commission to write guidelines for the counseling hotline [S2] [S3]. It never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Financial Services Committee until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Credit cardholders who carry a balance, especially those who pay only the minimum each month. Today's statements rarely show that a minimum-payment habit can stretch a single balance over decades and multiply the interest owed. The bill would have forced that math onto the front of every bill, shown the payment needed to be debt-free in three years, and provided a vetted counseling hotline staffed only by agencies meeting standards for independence, trained counselors, and reasonable fees [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Every monthly statement would have to carry a 'Minimum Payment Warning' showing, in years and months, how long it would take to pay off the balance at minimum payments, and the total cost broken down into principal and interest [S2] [S3].
Statements would show the monthly payment needed to eliminate the balance in 36 months, giving cardholders a concrete path out of debt instead of just a minimum figure [S2] [S3].

Statements would include a toll-free number for credit counseling and debt management, and the Federal Reserve and FTC could only approve nonprofit agencies that charge fair fees, use unbiased trained counselors, safeguard client funds, and pass independent accreditation [S3].

Disclosures must use the rate in effect when the statement is issued, and creditors with temporary or indexed rates must calculate warnings so the numbers reflect the rates cardholders will actually pay [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, who bear the cost of computing and printing the warnings on every statement and, more substantively, lose revenue if the disclosures lead more cardholders to pay above the minimum and pay balances off sooner, cutting the interest income that comes from long repayment periods [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: It is a disclosure-only fix: it does not cap interest rates, penalty fees, or minimum-payment levels, so cardholders still face the underlying debt trap even if they can see it spelled out [S2] [S3].
Issuers would face ongoing costs to calculate, print, and keep current the payoff projections on every statement, and some of that cost can be passed back to cardholders through fees or rates [S3].
Not every cardholder reads statement disclosures, so even a well-designed warning may change the behavior of only a portion of the people paying minimums [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: clearer information helps people who pay only the minimum understand the true cost, and the counseling referral comes with standards meant to screen out predatory agencies [S3]. The cost side is limited to issuer compliance and forgone interest, though the bill's weakness is that it informs rather than restrains — it leaves rates and fees untouched. As consumer-protective legislation goes, it is a small, low-risk improvement, and it never even got the chance to be tested [S5].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. David Price introduced the bill on March 13, 2007, with eight Democratic colleagues joining as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S1] [S3] [S5].
Fifteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total; no Republicans signed on [S4].

The Financial Services Committee took no further action — no markup, no hearing on the record, no vote — and the bill was never reported to the House floor before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers came out ahead: no minimum-payment warnings were required of them, and the interest revenue from cardholders who pay only the minimum was left untouched. Nonprofit credit counseling agencies also gained nothing, since the referral pipeline the bill would have created was never built.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, but the sponsorship record was one-sided: all 15 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on [S4].

industries.note: Issuers profit when cardholders pay only the minimum, stretching balances over years and multiplying interest. The bill would have shown every statement holder exactly that math and offered an escape payment and counseling line, costing issuers printing expenses and interest revenue [S2] [S3].

The bill would have routed cardholders to a toll-free counseling referral number, but only to agencies meeting the bill's standards for nonprofit status, unbiased counselors, fair fees, and accreditation [S3].
